classification.difficultyReason: Students distinguish the equal-dollar shift from the percentage alternative, explain why the shift preserves deviations, recompute the percentage-adjusted data using population statistics, and compare SDs. The explicit sequence supplies the route; calculating 15% introduces no additional conceptual demand.

content.prompt:
A cafe has five staff members. Their weekly wages are:
$\$380,\ \$460,\ \$520,\ \$620,\ \$780$

children.label: a
children.prompt: Calculate the population standard deviation for this set of data, rounded to the nearest dollar.

answer.worked:
Enter the five wages in the calculator's 1-variable statistics mode and select population standard deviation $\sigma_x$.
$$\begin{aligned}\sigma_x &\approx \$138.3329\\&\approx \$138\quad\text{(nearest dollar)}\end{aligned}$$

children.label: b
children.prompt: Each staff member receives a $\$25$ pay increase. Explain the effect that this increase will have on the standard deviation.

answer.short: Unchanged; the spread of the wages is unchanged.
answer.worked: Every wage and the mean increase by $\$25$, so each wage's distance from the mean stays the same. The standard deviation is unchanged.

children.label: c
children.prompt: Instead of the $\$25$ increase, every staff member receives a 15% pay rise. Calculate the new population standard deviation to the nearest dollar.

answer.worked:
New wages: $\$437,\ \$529,\ \$598,\ \$713,\ \$897$. Enter these in 1-variable statistics mode and select $\sigma_x$.
$$\begin{aligned}\sigma_x &\approx \$159.0828\\&\approx \$159\quad\text{(nearest dollar)}\end{aligned}$$

children.label: d
children.prompt: Which pay rise gives the smaller standard deviation: $\$25$ each or 15% each?

answer.worked: The $\$25$ pay rise leaves the standard deviation at approximately $\$138$. The 15% pay rise increases it to approximately $\$159$, so $\$25$ each gives the smaller standard deviation.
